title: JESUS SAID, “BE PERFECT.” BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN TERRIFIED OF WHAT HE ACTUALLY MEANT?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID, “BE PERFECT.” BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN TERRIFIED OF WHAT HE ACTUALLY MEANT?

The command that has haunted struggling Christians for centuries may be one of the most misunderstood invitations in the Sermon on the Mount. And when you discover what Jesus was really saying in the original Greek, you may never look at your failures, your enemies, or your Heavenly Father the same way again.
There is a particular kind of exhaustion that only a struggling Christian understands.
It is the exhaustion of loving Jesus while knowing you still have things in your heart that do not look like Him.
You pray. You repent. You promise yourself that this time will be different.
And then it happens again.
The anger you thought you had conquered returns. The temptation you swore you would never entertain finds another opening. The bitterness you buried begins speaking through your words.
You look at your Bible.
You remember everything God has done for you.
And somewhere between your disappointment and your shame, a verse comes back to haunt you.
“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.” — Matthew 5:48 (KJV)
Perfect?
Not better?
Not improving?
Not trying your best?
Perfect?
You stare at that word, and suddenly the Christian life feels like a mountain you were commanded to climb without ever being given the strength to reach the summit.
You begin wondering whether God is disappointed every time He looks at you.
Whether your repeated failures mean your repentance was never sincere.
Whether the fact that you are still struggling proves you were never truly changed.
And perhaps the most painful question of all begins forming in your heart.
What if I love Jesus, but I will never become the kind of person He commanded me to be?
If you have ever felt that fear, please do not rush past what comes next.
Because Jesus really did command His followers to be perfect.
We must not erase His words to make ourselves comfortable.
But we must also never separate His words from the conversation in which He spoke them.
And that conversation changes everything.
Jesus was standing before people who lived under the weight of religious expectations, social divisions, personal enemies, and the constant temptation to measure righteousness by outward appearances.
In Matthew 5, He was not offering a motivational speech about becoming the best version of yourself.
He was revealing the righteousness of the kingdom of heaven.
He confronted anger that grows into contempt.
Lust that begins before an outward act.
Promises made carelessly.
Retaliation disguised as justice.
And finally, He confronted something so deeply rooted in the human heart that even religious people could easily defend it.
The belief that love should be reserved for people who deserve it.
Listen carefully to what Jesus said immediately before the command to be perfect.
“Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy.” — Matthew 5:43 (KJV)
Here is an important distinction.
The command to love one's neighbor came from Scripture, particularly Leviticus 19:18.
But the command to hate one's enemy was not part of that verse.
Jesus was confronting a distorted understanding of love, one that allowed people to divide humanity into those worthy of compassion and those worthy of contempt.
And then He said something that must have stunned His listeners.
“But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.” — Matthew 5:44 (KJV)
Imagine hearing that while remembering someone who had deliberately humiliated you.
Someone who betrayed your trust.
Someone who spread lies about you.
Someone who walked away when you needed them most.
Jesus did not say that their actions were acceptable.
He did not say that evil should be ignored, that abuse should be tolerated, or that boundaries should disappear.
He said something far more challenging.
Do not allow another person's evil to become the pattern for your own heart.
And then Jesus pointed toward heaven.
He explained that the Father causes His sun to rise on both the evil and the good and sends rain on both the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45).
Think about that.
The same sunlight warms the home of the person who praises God and the person who curses His name.
The same rain falls upon the fields of those who worship Him and those who refuse to acknowledge Him.
God's ordinary kindness extends beyond the circle of those who love Him.
This does not mean God approves of wickedness. Scripture consistently teaches His holiness, justice, and coming judgment.
It means that even a rebellious world continues to receive undeserved gifts from its Creator.
And Jesus was saying that the children of this Father should increasingly reflect His character.
Then came the sentence that has frightened so many sincere believers.
“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.”
Notice the word therefore.
It matters.
Jesus was drawing a conclusion from everything He had just taught about love, mercy, and the Father's generous kindness.
He was not suddenly abandoning the subject to demand flawless performance in every imaginable human activity.
He was bringing His teaching about kingdom righteousness to its breathtaking conclusion.
To understand this, we need to look at the original language.
Matthew's Gospel preserves this teaching in Greek.
The word translated “perfect” is τέλειος (teleios).
In Matthew 5:48, the plural form is τέλειοι (teleioi), describing what Jesus commands His followers to be.
The word can mean perfect, complete, mature, or fully developed, depending on its context.
It is related to the Greek word telos, meaning an end, goal, or intended purpose.
But here is where careful interpretation matters.
It would be misleading to claim that teleios never means moral perfection or that Jesus was merely saying, “Just be a little more mature.”
The command is far too serious for that.
God Himself is the standard.
Yet the surrounding verses show us a particular expression of the perfection Jesus requires.
A love that does not stop at the boundaries of personal affection.
A love that refuses to become selective merely because someone is difficult, hostile, or undeserving.
A love that reflects the Father's generous character.
The point is not that the word teleios secretly means something entirely different from perfection.
The point is that Jesus defines the shape of this perfection through the Father's character and the radical love He has just commanded.
And there is another passage that makes this even clearer.
In Luke 6:36, within a closely related teaching about loving enemies, Jesus says:
“Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.” (KJV)
Matthew emphasizes being perfect as the Father is perfect.
Luke emphasizes being merciful as the Father is merciful.
These statements should not be flattened into identical definitions. They appear in distinct Gospel presentations, and each carries its own emphasis.
But together, they help us see the profound connection between the Father's character and the life Jesus calls His disciples to imitate.
The perfection Jesus commands cannot be separated from mercy.
And Christian maturity cannot be separated from love.
Suddenly, the question becomes much more uncomfortable.
Not merely, Have I avoided every mistake today?
But...
Am I becoming more like my Father in the way I treat people who cannot repay me?
Can I pray for someone who has wounded me without secretly hoping they will suffer?
Can I refuse revenge even when I have every opportunity to take it?
Can I speak truth without cruelty?
Can I love without pretending that sin is harmless?
Because sometimes the person who appears most religious is the very person whose heart has become hardest toward others.
And sometimes the person who knows how desperately they need mercy is the one most ready to extend it.
But there is still a problem.
A massive one.
Even when we understand the context, Jesus' command remains beyond our natural ability.
We cannot simply decide to become perfectly loving.
We cannot manufacture the holiness of God through stronger resolutions.
We cannot transform a sinful heart by promising harder.
And Scripture does not pretend otherwise.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
Not merely the visibly rebellious.
Not merely the people whose scandals became public.
All.
The respected church leader.
The faithful volunteer.
The exhausted mother.
The young believer battling temptation.
The person reading this article while quietly carrying a secret they have never told another soul.
All have sinned.
And if God's perfect righteousness is the standard, none of us can stand before Him boasting that we have reached it.
That is why the command of Jesus should never lead us into self-righteousness.
It should expose our need for a Savior.
And here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The One who commanded perfect righteousness is the very One who came to rescue people who could never establish their own.
Jesus Christ did not merely preach the Sermon on the Mount.
He lived the righteousness it reveals.
He loved without hypocrisy.
He obeyed the Father without rebellion.
He spoke truth without sin.
He showed compassion without compromising holiness.
And when His enemies mocked Him, rejected Him, and nailed Him to a cross, He demonstrated the very enemy-love He had commanded.
Luke 23:34 records His prayer:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
The hands that had healed the sick were pierced.
The mouth that had spoken life was surrounded by insults.
The One who deserved worship received cruelty.
And still, He prayed.
Do you see it?
The command to love your enemies was not merely a beautiful teaching delivered by someone safely removed from suffering.
Jesus embodied it in the midst of unimaginable suffering.
At Calvary, the perfect love of God was displayed in the sacrifice of His Son.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we conquered every temptation.
Not after we proved we could become respectable religious people.
While we were still sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Holy One died for the guilty.
The Righteous One gave Himself for the unrighteous.
And the sinners who could never earn salvation are invited to receive forgiveness through the crucified and risen Christ.
This is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is the beginning of a transformation we could never accomplish by ourselves.
The Gospel does not say that holiness no longer matters because Jesus died.
The Gospel says that because Jesus died and rose again, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed by His grace.
Listen to the difference.
Religion without grace says, “Become perfect so God will finally accept you.”
The Gospel announces that those who repent and trust in Jesus Christ are received through Him, not through the perfection of their personal record.
And the grace that saves them also begins teaching them to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 describes God's grace as bringing salvation and teaching us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires.
Grace is not merely pardon for yesterday.
It is also God's powerful work in the believer's life today.
That distinction matters because someone reading this is exhausted from confusing spiritual growth with earning God's love.
You have been measuring your relationship with Jesus by whether you managed to have a flawless week.
If you prayed consistently, resisted temptation, and controlled your temper, you felt worthy to approach Him.
But if you stumbled, you hid.
You delayed prayer.
You avoided Scripture.
You felt ashamed to worship.
As though the blood of Christ was sufficient for your conversion but somehow insufficient for your continued need of mercy.
Friend, hear this carefully.
Your failures must never become excuses for sin, but neither should they become reasons to run away from the only Savior who can cleanse you.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Confession is not pretending sin was small.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible because you were caught.
True repentance involves turning toward God, agreeing with His judgment about sin, and seeking to walk in obedience through His grace.
Sometimes it also requires confession to people we have harmed, restitution where possible, accountability, and difficult changes in our daily lives.
But repentance is not the purchase price of God's mercy.
Forgiveness is grounded in Jesus Christ and His saving work.
And the believer who has stumbled is not instructed to manufacture a perfect past.
They are called to come into the light.
This is where the original language of another passage gives us a beautiful perspective.
In Philippians 3:12, Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “perfect” in this verse is τετελείωμαι (teteleiōmai), a form of the verb teleioō, which is related to teleios.
Paul openly acknowledges that he has not already reached the final state of perfection.
Yet he does not use that admission as an excuse to stop pursuing Christ.
He presses forward.
Later, in Philippians 3:15, Paul uses τέλειοι (teleioi), often translated “perfect” or “mature,” when addressing believers who should share this Christ-centered outlook.
There is a meaningful distinction here.
Paul can speak of spiritual maturity while admitting that he has not yet reached the ultimate goal.
Christian maturity does not mean pretending you have already arrived.
It means pressing toward Christ with increasing humility, obedience, and dependence upon His grace.
And this is deeply important for understanding Matthew 5:48.
We must preserve the full seriousness of Jesus' command without confusing the believer's present growth with the final perfection God promises.
Hebrews 10:14 says:
“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.”
The verse holds together Christ's decisive sacrifice and the people who are being sanctified.
There is a finished work of Christ that believers must trust.
And there is an ongoing work of holiness that believers must not neglect.
These are not competing truths.
They belong together.
The Christian life is not a desperate attempt to become worthy of a Savior.
It is a life of faith and obedience flowing from the grace of the Savior who has already given Himself for us.
But perhaps you are thinking about something more personal.
You are not merely struggling with your own failures.
You are struggling with someone else's.
Someone who hurt you.
Someone who never apologized.
Someone who betrayed you and then behaved as though nothing happened.
You know Jesus commanded you to love your enemies.
But every time you remember what happened, something inside you tightens.
You want to forgive.
Then you remember the humiliation.
You want to pray.
Then you remember the lies.
You want to move forward.
Then the pain returns.
And suddenly Matthew 5:48 feels impossible again.
But consider what loving an enemy actually means.
It does not mean calling evil good.
It does not mean denying the damage someone caused.
It does not mean immediately restoring trust to someone who continues to violate it.
It does not require remaining in an abusive or dangerous situation.
Love can seek another person's ultimate good while maintaining wise boundaries and pursuing justice.
Forgiveness does not erase the need for accountability.
Jesus Himself confronted wrongdoing, exposed hypocrisy, and refused to entrust Himself indiscriminately to others (John 2:24).
So perhaps the first expression of enemy-love in your life will not be a dramatic reconciliation.
Perhaps it will be a quiet prayer.
“Father, I am still hurting. I do not know how to love this person rightly. But I do not want hatred to become my home. Teach me to respond in a way that honors You.”
That prayer may not instantly remove the pain.
But it can be an honest beginning.
And perhaps that is where God is confronting some of us today.
We have been asking Him to make us stronger while resisting His invitation to make us more merciful.
We have been asking for spiritual maturity while protecting bitterness.
We have been praying for a deeper relationship with Jesus while refusing to release our desire for revenge.
We want the comfort of being forgiven.
But we struggle with the cost of forgiving.
And the words of Jesus expose us.
“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.”
Not because He is indifferent to our weakness.
Not because He expects us to save ourselves.
But because the life of His kingdom is meant to reflect the character of our Heavenly Father.
This command does not become meaningless because we need grace to obey it.
It becomes a reason to depend upon grace more deeply.
And here is another truth we cannot overlook.
The perfection of God is not merely the perfection of His kindness toward enemies.
God is perfectly holy.
Perfectly righteous.
Perfectly truthful.
Perfectly just.
His love is never corrupt, and His mercy never requires Him to deny His holiness.
Therefore, becoming more like our Heavenly Father cannot mean becoming tolerant of everything or treating repentance as unnecessary.
Jesus calls us to love our enemies, and the same Jesus calls sinners to repent.
He offers mercy, and He warns of judgment.
He welcomes the broken, and He commands those who follow Him to deny themselves and take up their cross.
Biblical love and biblical holiness belong together.
That is why we must resist two dangerous distortions of Matthew 5:48.
One distortion says, “If you are not flawless, God has no place for you.”
The other says, “Since nobody is flawless, holiness does not matter.”
Both miss the Gospel.
The first forgets the sufficiency of Christ.
The second forgets the transforming purpose of His grace.
Jesus did not come to leave sinners trapped in condemnation.
And He did not come to leave them comfortably enslaved to sin.
He came to save.
To forgive.
To redeem.
To transform.
To make a people who increasingly reflect His character.
Second Corinthians 3:18 describes believers being changed into the Lord's image from glory to glory by the Spirit.
That transformation is real.
It may be gradual.
It may involve painful correction.
It may require repeatedly surrendering attitudes you once defended.
But it is not imaginary.
The Holy Spirit does not merely teach Christians to sound more religious.
He produces fruit.
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Longsuffering.
Gentleness.
Goodness.
Faith.
Meekness.
Temperance.
These qualities, described in Galatians 5:22–23, are not decorations added to an otherwise unchanged life.
They are evidence of the Spirit's work.
And sometimes the clearest evidence of spiritual growth is not that you never feel anger.
It is that you no longer surrender to anger as easily.
Not that you never experience temptation.
But that you increasingly learn to resist it and flee toward Christ.
Not that you never feel wounded.
But that you are learning to bring your wounds before God instead of allowing them to become weapons against other people.
Not that you never need forgiveness.
But that you are becoming quicker to confess, quicker to repent, and less willing to hide.
And one day, the work God has begun will reach its promised completion.
First John 3:2 says:
“Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.”
What a promise.
We are not yet what we shall be.
But those who belong to Christ have a future that is not defined by the permanence of their present weaknesses.
The hope of Christian perfection is not ultimately confidence in our ability to improve ourselves.
It is confidence in the Savior who redeems His people and will complete His work.
Philippians 1:6 reminds believers that the One who began a good work in them will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.
So when Jesus says, “Be perfect,” we must neither soften His standard nor despair as though He has offered no salvation.
We must look to the Father whose character He commands us to reflect.
We must look honestly at the sin that still lives in us.
And above all, we must look to Jesus Christ.
The One who fulfilled righteousness.
The One who loved His enemies.
The One who carried our sins.
The One who died and rose again.
The One who calls us to repentance and faith.
The One who gives His Spirit to those who belong to Him.
And the One who will not abandon His saving purpose.
Maybe you have spent years believing that your greatest problem was that you were not perfect enough for Jesus.
But the deeper problem was never something you could solve by trying harder without Him.
You needed redemption.
You needed forgiveness.
You needed a new heart.
You needed grace.
And you still need Him today.
Not less than you did when you first believed.
Every single day.
So here is a question I want you to sit with.
If someone examined the way you treat the people who have hurt you, would they see anything of your Heavenly Father's mercy?
If someone watched the way you respond after you sin, would they see genuine repentance or a cycle of hiding and excuses?
If someone listened to the way you speak about people you dislike, would they hear the voice of someone being transformed by Jesus?
These are not questions meant to crush the repentant believer.
They are invitations to examine our hearts in the light of God's Word.
Because sometimes we spend so much time asking whether God has forgiven our past that we forget to ask what He wants to transform in our present.
And perhaps the most important response you can make today is not to promise Jesus that you will never fail again.
Perhaps it is to stop defending what He has been calling you to surrender.
The bitterness.
The secret sin.
The pride.
The spiritual performance.
The resentment.
The belief that you must hide your weakness before you can approach Him.
Bring it into the light.
Call sin what Scripture calls it.
Trust the finished work of Jesus Christ.
Ask the Holy Spirit to change what your own strength has failed to change.
And then walk in obedience, one faithful step at a time.
Not to purchase the Father's love.
But because, through Christ, you have encountered a love that changes people.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to reveal private details to strangers. Sometimes a simple confession of dependence on God can encourage another believer who thought they were struggling alone.
And if you have a testimony about how Christ helped you release bitterness, repent of sin, or grow in mercy, consider sharing it.
Someone reading the comments may need to be reminded that transformation through Jesus Christ is possible.
There is also someone in your circle who needs this message.
Perhaps a believer who has become exhausted by perfectionism.
A friend who believes one terrible mistake has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
A family member who has quietly drifted away from faith.
Or someone who has never understood why Christians speak so passionately about grace.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because someone you know may be asking the very question this article addresses.
Because the struggle between shame and grace is not always settled by reading one message.
Sometimes we need to return to Scripture again and again until the truth begins shaping the way we think, pray, repent, forgive, and live.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish emotionally moving articles, but to help people encounter biblical truth, grow in discipleship, and continually return to Jesus Christ.

We want this community to become a place where Scripture is taken seriously, where sin is not excused, where wounded people are treated with compassion, and where Jesus Christ remains at the center of everything.
And for those who want to help us continue and expand this mission, there is another meaningful way to participate.
Scripture teaches that believers may support those who labor in teaching the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14), and that giving should be willing rather than pressured (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And we want to express our appreciation in a practical way.
It is participating in an ongoing effort to make Christ-centered encouragement and biblical discipleship more accessible.
We want people to grow in their understanding of Scripture, deepen their relationship with Christ, and become equipped to share the Gospel with others.
Pray for this ministry.
Invite someone to read the Scriptures.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Tell someone what Jesus Christ has done for you.
These are meaningful ways to serve the Gospel.
Because the mission is not ultimately about building a platform.
It is about pointing people to the Savior.
And before you leave, I want to bring you back to the question that started this entire conversation.
What did Jesus mean when He said we must be perfect as our Heavenly Father is perfect?
He was calling His disciples to the complete, holy, wholehearted love that reflects the character of their Father, especially a love that reaches beyond friends and extends even toward enemies.
He was not giving us permission to settle for sin.
Nor was He teaching that we could earn salvation through flawless performance.
He was revealing the righteousness of God's kingdom, a standard that exposes our need for grace and a way of life into which Christ calls those who follow Him.
The standard is not lowered.
The Savior is exalted.
And through the grace of Jesus Christ and the work of the Holy Spirit, those who belong to Him are being transformed toward the likeness of the One who saved them.
So do not walk away from Matthew 5:48 believing that Jesus has simply demanded the impossible and left you alone to accomplish it.
Walk away humbled by the holiness of God.
Convicted by the depth of His command.
Grateful for the cross.
Dependent upon His Spirit.
And ready to take your next step of obedience.
Because the same Jesus who said, “Be ye therefore perfect,” also said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28 (KJV)
He never invited us to make peace with our sin.
But He did invite weary sinners to come to Him.
And that invitation still stands.
So come.
Not pretending you have already arrived.
Not demanding that God accept the sins you refuse to surrender.
Not trusting your religious achievements.
Come in repentance and faith.
Come to the crucified and risen Christ.
Come to the Savior whose mercy is greater than anything you could ever deserve.
And let His grace begin changing the places in your heart that you once believed could never change.
Your past may explain the scars you carry, but in Christ, it does not have to write the final sentence of your story.
